title: Put cameras in context with floor plans
description: Understand indoor camera placements, safe plan changes and the access inherited from a site.

chapters.title: Start with a site's indoor picture

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Let's take a fictional warehouse with several corridors. Camera names are useful, but the team wants to see which entrance each camera covers. How does a floor plan help?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A floor plan is an indoor image attached to a site. You upload the plan from that site's detail page, then place the site's cameras on it. It adds spatial context without creating a separate camera system.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Is it a whole new top-level page to learn?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Management starts inside the site. The deployment must enable the floor-plan feature, and the guide gives the image requirements. Choose a clean, correctly oriented plan so people can recognise rooms and entrances.

chapters.title: A marker is not a new device

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Our operator places the entrance camera on the plan. What connects that marker to the real camera?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: You choose a device belonging to the current site and save its placement. Its position uses relative image coordinates, so resizing the view doesn't move it to a different room. A device appears only once on the same plan.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What if the marker is wrong and we remove it?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Removing the placement removes the marker, not the camera. It doesn't disconnect or delete the device. That's an important distinction when you're tidying a diagram rather than changing the monitoring equipment.

chapters.title: Review changes to the underlying image

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The warehouse layout changes. Can we replace the image and assume the old markers still point to the right places?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Review them afterward. A replacement image may have a different crop, orientation or shape. A name-only change preserves the current image and placements, but the system can't infer how a new drawing relates to the old one.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: That removes the plan and its placements, not the devices. External image cleanup can happen asynchronously. A short delay in removing a stored image doesn't mean the deleted plan is still available in Hub.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can anyone who discovers the plan manage it?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Plans inherit access from their site, within the current account and project context. Management follows the site's edit permissions. A helpful diagram doesn't replace access control.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Start with one clear plan and one camera you can verify physically. Save it, check the placement, then add the rest. If an uploaded image is blank, check the documented storage-origin policy rather than moving all the markers at random.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
